strengths: Significance: Improving the reliability of LLM-generated architecture edits is a useful problem when candidate training is expensive. Explicitly selecting an editable region and checking feasibility before training is a practical approach.

Method and presentation: Algorithms 1–2 and Section 3.3 clearly describe routing, refinement, and enforcement through normalized diffs, region preservation, and interface/shape checks. These provide a concrete starting point for implementation.

Empirical promise: Table 1 reports substantial improvements on DFS, articulation points, and connected components with similar reported MACs. Transferring a DFS-discovered architecture to other tasks is a useful evaluation direction, and the two-editor ablation provides some evidence that the approach is not specific to one LLM.
Transparency and ethics: The appendix includes architecture listings and results showing substantial negative transfer on some tasks. The work presents no apparent material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—implementation contradicts the central constraint: Section 3 requires every accepted edit to change only one factor while preserving interfaces. However, Listing 2, labeled iteration 1, changes both the initialization and computation functions relative to the sole initial architecture in Listing 1: it introduces self.heads and rewrites computation to consume it. This cannot be the first accepted single-factor edit under the stated procedure. Listing 5 also adds an adj_mat argument despite the frozen-signature requirement. These contradictions directly undermine whether the evaluated implementation follows SPARK; parent-linked traces and actual feasibility-check outputs are needed.

Soundness—held-out evaluation is not established: Equation 1 uses OOD accuracy as fitness, the archive includes ood_acc, and Section 4.2 reports selecting the best architecture using the CLRS OOD split. No separate search-validation and final test sets are specified. Repeatedly optimizing the reported OOD split risks adaptive test-set overfitting, so the headline generalization result needs an untouched final evaluation.

Soundness—the 28.1× efficiency claim is unsupported by consistent accounting: Section 4.2 equates proposal attempt 57 with 57 evaluated candidates, but Figure 2c shows a cumulative valid rate near one-half at that point. Under the paper's definitions, these cannot both describe the same trajectory. The 1600/57 comparison also combines EvoPrompting's separate experimental setting with the present run without establishing matched editors, training costs, or time-to-target performance. A candidate-count ratio is insufficient to establish the advertised speedup.

Evidence and presentation contain unresolved discrepancies: Figure 2a shows OpenEvolve reaching roughly 56% rather than the 32.54% in Table 1, without explaining a different run or aggregation. Figure A.1's five-seed best-so-far OOD curves finish around 0.22–0.25 and do not identify a task or normalization that reconciles them with 83.74% DFS accuracy. The main text describes 18-task supplementary results, whereas Table A.1 contains 30 tasks; Table 1's CC is labeled SCC in the appendix. These inconsistencies prevent a reliable interpretation of the reported evidence.

Originality and causal attribution remain limited: Factor-restricted editing is a plausible adaptation of structured mutation and code editing, but reduced syntactic cross-region editing does not itself demonstrate reduced functional interference. The ablations do not adequately specify how ASR-only and RC+SAR-only generate and constrain edits. Random or alternating factor selection, matched feasibility checks, and a simple scoped-edit baseline are needed to distinguish the proposed routing/directive mechanism from generic restrictions, filtering, or additional LLM calls.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite useful pseudocode and listings: The manuscript omits complete role prompts, precise training hyperparameters and data-split specifications, baseline adaptation details, software versions, and a runnable implementation. Main tables lack uncertainty estimates, and the five-seed appendix does not resolve variability in the principal comparisons. Reporting MACs as model size and attributing their overhead to the editing interface also needs clarification: search-time editing does not inherently add inference computation.

Significance and limitations need more balanced interpretation: Search is demonstrated only on DFS within one architecture family. The ten-task main table favors SPARK throughout, while the broader appendix reports severe regressions, including BFS from 99.7% to 70.6% and Floyd–Warshall from 48.5% to 32.9%. Disclosing these results is valuable, but task-selection rationale, full-suite aggregate performance, and analysis of negative transfer are needed to support broad robustness claims. The promising idea does not outweigh the unresolved methodological and evidential problems.

strengths: Significance: Improving the reliability of LLM-generated architecture edits is a useful problem when training candidates is expensive. Explicit edit scopes and inexpensive feasibility checks offer a practical approach.

Method and presentation: Sections 3.2–3.3 give understandable pseudocode, define factor-local edits, and specify normalization and checks for preserving unchanged regions. These details make the intended mechanism reasonably clear.

Empirical promise: Table 1 reports substantial gains on DFS and several transfer tasks at similar reported inference MACs. Searching on DFS and retraining the resulting architecture on other tasks is a useful test of architectural transfer.

Evaluation breadth and ethics: The manuscript includes ablations with two LLM editors, a five-seed search figure, architecture listings, and broader results that disclose performance regressions. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described application.
weaknesses: Soundness—implementation contradicts the central constraint: The method requires each accepted edit to change only Operator or Action while preserving the other region byte-for-byte. However, Listings 1–2 show iteration 1 replacing the Operator's individual projections with a ModuleList and simultaneously rewriting the Action to use those heads. This first transition from the sole seed changes both factors. Listing 5 also adds an adj_mat argument despite the stated frozen-signature requirement. These examples require reconciliation before the reported results can be attributed to the specified algorithm.

Soundness—unsupported headline efficiency: Section 4.2 identifies proposal attempt 57 with 57 evaluated candidates, but Figure 2c shows a cumulative valid rate of approximately 0.5 around that point. Under the stated accounting, these cannot describe the same trajectory. Moreover, dividing EvoPrompting's 1600-evaluation budget by SPARK's best-result index does not establish a controlled speedup without matching the target accuracy, editor, evaluator, and search setting. Sections 4 and 4.2 also disagree about whether EvoPrompting uses multitask evolution or the common 100-attempt DFS protocol.

Soundness—unclear separation of search and test data: Equation 1 uses OOD accuracy as fitness, Section 4 includes ood_acc in archive descriptors, and Section 4.2 selects the incumbent using the CLRS OOD split. No independent final test split is identified. Repeated selection on the reported OOD split risks adaptive overfitting; a separate search-validation split and untouched test evaluation are needed to support the generalization claims.

Evidence and presentation—results do not reconcile: Figure A.1's five-seed best-so-far OOD accuracies plateau near 0.22–0.25, without an explanation connecting them to the headline 83.74%. Figure 2a shows OpenEvolve reaching roughly 57%, whereas Table 1 reports 32.54% on DFS. The main text describes 18 tasks, but Table A.1 contains 30; Table 1's Connected Components row becomes Strongly Connected Components in the appendix. These discrepancies materially obscure which experiments support the conclusions.

Originality and causal attribution: Factor-scoped editing is a plausible application of structured mutation and constrained code editing, but the claimed new understanding of functional entanglement is not established. The metric measures cross-region text changes, not functional interference, and its reduction is directly encouraged by the method's constraints. There is no random or alternating scope baseline with the same checks, or matched local-edit baseline without the router/directive machinery. The ASR-only and RC+SAR-only implementations are insufficiently specified. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate knowledge activation from simpler scope restrictions, extra prompting, or feasibility filtering.

Reproducibility: Exact role prompts, training hyperparameters, split construction, implementation versions, complete parent–offspring logs, and executable feasibility tests are not supplied. Main tables lack uncertainty estimates and do not identify whether entries are best runs or averages. The five-seed figure does not resolve this ambiguity. Reported inference MACs also do not measure search cost: SPARK uses routing, directive, and editing calls, but LLM token costs and end-to-end runtime are absent.

Significance and limitations: The evidence is confined to one architecture family and DFS-based search. The selected ten-task average highlights favorable transfer, while Table A.1 shows substantial regressions on BFS (99.7% to 70.6%) and Floyd–Warshall (48.5% to 32.9%). Reporting these failures is valuable, but the main claims need a balanced aggregate and analysis of when the factorization helps or hurts. The useful underlying idea does not outweigh the unresolved methodological and evidential inconsistencies, so I recommend rejection.

strengths: Significance: Making LLM-generated architecture edits more reliable is a useful research objective when candidate training is expensive. Explicit edit scopes and inexpensive feasibility checks form a practical, understandable approach.

Originality: Separating Operator definitions from Action composition provides a concrete NAS-specific application of structured editing. Combining scope selection, feedback-conditioned directives, and constrained refinement is a potentially useful contribution, even though the individual ingredients are established.

Empirical promise: Table 1 reports substantial improvements on DFS (83.74% versus 46.78% for CLRS) and several transfer tasks, with similar reported MACs. Searching on DFS and retraining the discovered architecture on other tasks is a valuable test of architectural transfer.

Presentation and ethics: The main method includes explicit pseudocode, a formal locality constraint, and a reasonably clear feasibility pipeline. The appendix supplies architecture examples and reports transfer failures as well as successes. No material research-ethics concern is evident for this benchmark-based study.
weaknesses: Soundness—implementation contradicts the central constraint: Section 3.3 requires the non-selected region to remain byte-identical and interfaces to remain unchanged. However, the transition from Iteration 0 to Iteration 1 in Listings 1–2 changes both the Operator, replacing individual projections with a ModuleList, and the Action, replacing the computation with a head loop and interaction terms. Listing 5 also adds an adj_mat argument absent from the original signature. These examples need reconciliation with the claimed enforcement; otherwise, the supplied architecture trajectory does not demonstrate the stated method.

Soundness—evaluation accounting is inconsistent: Section 4.2 identifies proposal attempt 57 with 57 evaluated candidates. Yet Figure 2c shows a cumulative valid rate near one-half around that attempt, implying substantially fewer evaluations under the paper's definition. The headline 28.1× figure therefore lacks a consistent denominator. Moreover, comparing SPARK's best result with EvoPrompting's total 1600-evaluation budget is not a matched time-to-target comparison, and does not establish an equivalent computational speedup.

Soundness—reported results cannot currently be reconciled: Figure A.1a presents five-seed best-so-far OOD accuracies that plateau around 0.22–0.25, without explaining their relationship to the headline 83.74% DFS result. Figure 2a shows OpenEvolve reaching roughly 56%, whereas Table 1 reports 32.54% for its best transferred DFS architecture. The main text and conclusion discuss 18 tasks, while Table A.1 contains 30; the main table also labels a task CC while the appendix labels matching results SCC. These are material reporting inconsistencies rather than cosmetic errors.

Evaluation validity: The evaluator, archive descriptors, and best-candidate selection explicitly use OOD accuracy, but the manuscript does not establish an independent held-out OOD test set separate from search feedback. If the reported OOD split is repeatedly used for architecture selection, the final DFS accuracy is adaptively selected on that split. A clear validation/test separation and independent final evaluation are necessary to support the generalization claim.

Causal evidence and originality: Reduced cross-region editing follows directly from the imposed locality rule; it does not by itself establish reduced functional interference or improved knowledge activation. Table 2 does not adequately define how 'ASR only' generates edits or how 'RC+SAR only' chooses its scope. Random or alternating scope selection, constrained editing without the directive module, and matched feasibility filtering would help distinguish intelligent routing from generic output restriction and additional LLM calls.

Reproducibility: The manuscript gives the editor version, temperature, and some archive settings, but omits actual role prompts, precise training settings, baseline adaptation details, and several search configuration values. It is also unclear whether EvoPrompting numbers are rerun under the stated common 100-attempt protocol or taken from its original multi-task, 1600-evaluation setting. Main tables lack seed variability, and the appendix's unexplained accuracy scale prevents its five-seed figure from resolving robustness concerns.

Significance and limitations: Evidence is limited to evolution of one CLRS module on DFS. Table A.1 shows substantial negative transfer, including BFS falling from 99.7% to 70.6% and Floyd–Warshall from 48.5% to 32.9%. Reporting these failures is valuable, but the favorable ten-task headline needs a selection rationale and an aggregate over the complete reported suite. Similar inference MACs also do not establish similar total search cost; proposal, routing, directive, and training costs are not jointly accounted for. The promising specialized contribution is outweighed by unresolved issues in its central evidence.

strengths: Significance: Improving the reliability of LLM-generated architecture edits is a useful problem. The reported search-and-transfer results are promising: SPARK achieves 83.91% mean accuracy across 30 CLRS tasks versus 80.89% for EvoPrompting, with substantial improvements on DFS and SCC.

Originality: Explicitly separating operator definitions from their invocation and combining scope selection, refinement directives, and feasibility checks provides a concrete NAS-specific structured-editing approach. Appendix A.4 includes useful random-scope, fixed-scope, and component-removal controls.

Presentation: The algorithms and feasibility rules make the intended procedure understandable. The limitations appropriately acknowledge manual factor definitions, additional LLM calls, and transfer failures. No material research-ethics concern is evident from the described benchmark applications.
weaknesses: Soundness—implementation contradicts the central constraint. Sections 3.2–3.3 require each accepted edit to change only one region while preserving interfaces. However, the transition from Iteration 0 to Iteration 1 in Listings 1–2 replaces the operator definitions with self.heads and simultaneously rewrites the action to consume them. This cannot be the first accepted factor-local edit from the stated seed. Listing 5 also adds an adj_mat argument absent from the original signature. Actual parent–offspring diffs and feasibility logs are needed to establish that the evaluated implementation follows the proposed method.

Soundness—held-out evaluation is unclear. Equation 1 uses OOD accuracy as fitness, Section 4.2 evaluates search progress on the CLRS OOD split, and the archive includes ood_acc. The manuscript does not identify a separate, untouched OOD test set for final reporting. As written, architecture selection appears to reuse the reported evaluation split, leaving the DFS generalization claim vulnerable to adaptive selection bias.

The headline 28.1× efficiency claim has inconsistent accounting. Section 4.2 equates proposal attempt 57 with 57 evaluated candidates, while Figure 2c shows only roughly half of proposals are valid near that point. These cannot describe the same trajectory under the stated definitions. Moreover, dividing EvoPrompting's total 1600-evaluation budget by SPARK's selected stopping point does not establish matched-target efficiency without EvoPrompting's corresponding learning curve and comparable experimental conditions.

Reported results are internally inconsistent. Figure 2a shows OpenEvolve reaching approximately 57% best-so-far accuracy, whereas Table 1 reports 32.54% on DFS. Figure A.1a labels its five-seed results as best-so-far OOD accuracy but plateaus around 0.22–0.24, without explaining its relationship to the headline 83.74%. The main tables and ablations lack uncertainty estimates and do not clearly distinguish selected-run results from averages over search and training seeds.

Reproducibility is inadequate for resolving these issues. The abstract's code-availability statement has no link; exact role prompts, complete training settings, baseline adaptations, and several archive settings are missing. Appendix A.5 lists additional benchmarks without specifying their splits, preprocessing, editable regions, or training protocols. Consequently, the large MNIST-1D gains and small improvements on other datasets cannot be assessed reliably.

The mechanism and originality claims exceed the evidence. A line-based cross-region edit metric measures compliance with the imposed constraint, not functional interference itself. The ablations are useful but do not establish that reduced semantic entanglement causes the gains rather than additional prompting or constrained exploration. Likewise, comparable MACs do not establish comparable capacity, and Table 1's attribution of inference overhead to the editing interface is unexplained. The potentially useful contribution is structured scope control, but its stronger causal interpretation remains unsupported.

strengths: Significance: Improving the reliability of LLM-generated architecture edits is a useful problem. SPARK provides a concrete mechanism combining scope selection, refinement directives, localized editing, and inexpensive feasibility checks.

Empirical merits: The reported full-suite CLRS improvement (83.91% versus 80.89% for EvoPrompting) and transfer from DFS to other tasks are promising. Appendix A.4 includes relevant random-scope, fixed-scope, and component ablations, extending the evaluation beyond a comparison with unrestricted rewriting.

Presentation: The method's high-level workflow, region enforcement, and proposal-versus-evaluation distinction are clearly described through equations and pseudocode. The program listings provide concrete examples of architectural changes.

Limitations and ethics: The paper appropriately acknowledges transfer failures, additional LLM costs, and manually defined factors. These disclosures are valuable, and no material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described applications.
weaknesses: Soundness—selection and testing are not adequately separated. Section 4.2 explicitly uses the CLRS OOD split to measure search performance, while the evaluator and archive use OOD accuracy as feedback. No independent held-out DFS evaluation is described after architecture selection. Consequently, the headline DFS result may reflect adaptive selection on the reported evaluation set rather than independently measured OOD generalization. Cross-task transfer is useful evidence but does not resolve this issue.

Soundness—the 28.1× efficiency claim has inconsistent accounting. Section 4.2 equates proposal attempt 57 with 57 evaluated candidates, but Figure 2c shows only approximately half of proposals valid around that point. These cannot describe the same trajectory under the stated definitions. Moreover, dividing EvoPrompting's total 1600-evaluation budget by SPARK's selected stopping point is not a controlled comparison of evaluations needed to reach a common accuracy target. The paper also alternates between describing all methods as using 100 attempts and describing EvoPrompting as using its original multi-task search setting.

Soundness—the supplied evolution trace conflicts with the defining constraint. Listings 1 and 2, labeled iterations 0 and 1, change both operator definitions and action code: individual projections become a ModuleList of heads, and the forward computation changes to consume those heads. This violates the single-region, frozen-other-region rule. Listing 5 additionally introduces an adj_mat argument absent from the original signature, despite the stated signature invariants. The manuscript needs to reconcile these examples with the actual enforced search procedure.

Evidence and presentation—major numerical inconsistencies remain unexplained. Figure A.1's five-seed best-so-far OOD curves finish around 0.22–0.25, whereas the central DFS result is 83.74%. Figure 2a shows OpenEvolve reaching roughly 56%, but Table 1 reports 32.54%. Several reported search results also fall below the evaluated initial seed despite an archive that should retain the best candidate; independent retraining could explain this, but such a distinction is not documented. These discrepancies prevent a reliable interpretation of the reported performance.

Originality and mechanism: The useful novelty is primarily the integration of scope routing and directive generation with constrained code editing. The stronger claim of resolving functional entanglement is not established: syntactic locality does not ensure functional independence between module definitions and their uses. Lower cross-region edit frequency is partly encouraged by construction, and the heuristic feasibility argument assumes independence without evidence. The scope-control ablations are relevant, but lack uncertainty estimates and controls matching LLM-call or token budgets.

Reproducibility and significance: The abstract's code link is blank, and exact role prompts, training configurations, split construction, software versions, and non-CLRS factor definitions are missing. Main results and ablations lack clearly specified seed aggregation and variability; the five-seed figure does not reconcile with the tables. Appendix A.5 mostly reports results rather than a reproducible benchmark protocol. Small gains such as 97.04% versus 96.90% on BCW and 489.00 versus 488.65 on CartPole cannot establish meaningful superiority without uncertainty estimates. Overall, the promising approach requires substantial evidential reconciliation before others can reliably build on it.

strengths: Significance: Improving the reliability of LLM-generated architecture edits is a useful problem. Explicit scope selection, scoped refinement, and inexpensive feasibility checks form a practical approach to reducing wasted training evaluations.

Originality: The OPERATOR/ACTION decomposition offers a concrete application of structured editing to NAS. Appendix A.4 goes beyond component removal by comparing random and fixed scopes, providing useful evidence for adaptive routing and directive generation.

Empirical promise: The reported gains are substantial, including 83.74% DFS accuracy and 83.91% average accuracy across 30 CLRS tasks. Searching on DFS and transferring the architecture to other tasks is an interesting evaluation design. Additional benchmarks and a second LLM editor broaden the investigation.

Presentation and limitations: The main algorithm and feasibility rules are explicitly described. The paper appropriately acknowledges transfer failures, additional LLM-call costs, and manually defined factors. These candid limitations are valuable, and no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—evaluation independence: Section 4.2 explicitly uses the CLRS OOD split to measure search performance, while Section 3 defines performance as fitness and Section 4 includes ood_acc in archive descriptors. No separate OOD validation and untouched final test split is identified. Consequently, the headline DFS result appears to be adaptively selected on the reported evaluation distribution; independent held-out evaluation is needed to support the generalization claim.

Soundness—implementation contradicts the central constraint: Section 3.3 requires the unselected region to remain byte-identical and interfaces to remain fixed. However, Listings 1 and 2, labeled iterations 0 and 1, change both operator definitions and action code, replacing individual projections with self.heads and changing their invocation. Listing 5 also adds an adj_mat argument absent from the seed signature. These examples do not demonstrate the stated feasible editing process. Actual parent–offspring traces and enforcement logs are necessary to establish which algorithm produced the results.

Soundness—efficiency accounting is inconsistent: Section 4.2 states that proposal attempt 57 corresponds to 57 evaluated candidates, but Figure 2c shows cumulative validity near 0.5 around that point. Under the stated definitions, those quantities cannot both be 57 for the same trajectory. Moreover, the 28.1× ratio compares against EvoPrompting's 1600-evaluation setting without establishing matched editors, protocols, or time-to-target. The manuscript also alternates between describing all methods as using 100 DFS attempts and EvoPrompting as searching multiple tasks. These ambiguities undermine a central headline claim.

Presentation and evidential consistency: Figure 2a shows OpenEvolve reaching roughly 57% best-so-far accuracy, whereas Table 1 reports 32.54%. Figure A.1a, presented as five-seed CLRS search evidence, finishes around 0.22–0.25 OOD accuracy without identifying a task or explaining its relationship to the 83.74% result. These discrepancies prevent the figures from substantiating the reported performance and robustness.

Reproducibility and uncertainty: The abstract's code-availability statement has no link. Exact role prompts, executable region-tagged templates, baseline adaptations, and detailed training and data-split configurations are missing. Most performance and ablation tables provide no uncertainty or clear aggregation across search and training seeds. The five-seed figure does not resolve this, particularly given its unexplained accuracy scale. Small additional-benchmark gains therefore remain inconclusive.

Mechanistic evidence and originality: The entanglement metric measures cross-region textual edits, not functional interference; changing one region can still alter behavior throughout the program. Lower measured entanglement is partly enforced by construction. Although the scope-control ablations are useful, they do not isolate the claimed mechanism from extra LLM calls and richer feedback under matched resource budgets. The demonstrated novelty is primarily an engineering combination of scoped editing, routing, and feasibility filtering.

Significance and cost support: Comparable final-model MACs do not establish comparable search cost or explain why accuracy improves. Table 1's attribution of inference-compute overhead to the editing interface is unclear, and CLRS search-time and LLM-call totals are not supplied. Full-suite comparisons also omit the strongest controlled search baselines. The promising contribution needs a reconciled, reproducible evaluation before its claimed efficiency and generality can be relied upon.
